title: The Recovery You Bring Home
author: Camilo Zambrano
summary: Camilo Zambrano uses an upcoming family vacation to ask what people are really escaping when they travel. Drawing on Marcus Aurelius and Lucretius, he suggests people are not fleeing themselves but the environment and cues of daily life, a point supported by a survey of tourists whose top motives were new experiences and getting away from the normal environment. Vacations start recovery but do not sustain it, since studies find burnout can rebound within days and return to pre-vacation levels in about three weeks. Zambrano then separates peace of mind from happiness, treating it as a relatively stable internal state that contributes to subjective well-being and to resisting what he calls drift. He links this to equanimity, the ability to return to an emotional baseline, and frames practicing it as a form of discipline. His advice is to use vacations as checkpoints for continued recovery, not as rescue operations.
points: People take vacations to change the environment that shapes them, not to escape reality or themselves, so detachment from daily cues is what enables recovery to begin.
Recovery from vacation fades quickly, and chasing the next getaway can become a cycle of resets instead of cumulative progress.
Peace of mind is a stable internal state in spite of disturbances, and it contributes to well-being without being the same as happiness.
Equanimity, the ability to return to your emotional baseline after disruption, is presented as a trainable form of discipline and a defense against drift.
Treat time away as a checkpoint from which recovery continues at home, and plan for how you will keep returning to yourself afterward.
quotes: My interpretation of this boils down to the idea that those who travel to escape are not really escaping. What they’re looking for is to find peace elsewhere, when many times peace needs to be found within yourself.

Okay, so when people want to escape, they are not trying to escape from themselves. They are trying to escape, momentarily, from the environment that wraps around their everyday lives, to experience life differently from how they would otherwise.
But recovery doesn’t happen in a day. It does start very quickly after you take a vacation, but studies have found that, once you return, issues like burnout can begin to rebound within days.
How can we make recovery sustainable and use vacations as checkpoints that help us build on recovery, rather than as reset points that take us back to zero every time?
Science describes it more closely as having a relatively stable internal state; it’s more associated with the existence of that stable internal state in spite of those disturbances.

Developing equanimity means developing the ability to reduce how strongly disturbances govern you. As you learn this ability, you start learning to return to your emotional baseline when life disrupts it.
Once it has started, your goal should not be to make vacations the next rescue operation, but to use them as checkpoints from which recovery can continue.
